questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Following graph shows four different processes, adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric for an ideal gas, from the same initial state. Study the graph carefully and state which of the following statements is correct?
questions.solution:
From the given $P-V$ graph, we can analyze the four processes starting from the same initial state:

1. Process 1 is a vertical line parallel to the $P$-axis. This indicates that the volume $V$ remains constant while the pressure changes. Therefore, Process 1 is an isochoric process.

2. Process 4 is a horizontal line parallel to the $V$-axis. This indicates that the pressure $P$ remains constant while the volume changes. Therefore, Process 4 is an isobaric process.

3. Processes 2 and 3 are curves representing expansion (volume increases and pressure decreases). We know that the magnitude of the slope of an adiabatic curve on a $P-V$ diagram is $\gamma$ times the magnitude of the slope of an isothermal curve $\left( \left| \dfrac{dP}{dV} \right|_{\text{adiabatic}} = \gamma \dfrac{P}{V} \text{ and } \left| \dfrac{dP}{dV} \right|_{\text{isothermal}} = \dfrac{P}{V} \right). Since \gamma >1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve. Thus, the steeper curve 2 is the adiabatic process, and curve 3 is the isothermal process.

Evaluating the given options:
(A) Process 4 is adiabatic - Incorrect (it is isobaric).
(B) Process 1 is isochoric - Correct.
(C) Process 2 is isobaric - Incorrect (it is adiabatic).
(D) Process 3 is isochoric - Incorrect (it is isothermal).

Answer: Process 1 is isochoric

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two vessels A and B contain same mass of Oxygen and Hydrogen respectively at the same temperature. The volume of B is twice that of A. The ratio of gas pressure in A to that in B is
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT = \dfrac{m}{M}RT$, where $m$ is the given mass and $M$ is the molar mass.

For vessel A containing Oxygen ($O_2$, $M_A = 32$):
$P_A = \dfrac{mRT}{32 V_A}$

For vessel B containing Hydrogen ($H_2$, $M_B = 2$):
$P_B = \dfrac{mRT}{2 V_B}$

Given that the volume of B is twice that of A ($V_B = 2V_A$), we get:
$P_B = \dfrac{mRT}{2(2V_A)} = \dfrac{mRT}{4V_A}$

Taking the ratio of the pressures:
$\dfrac{P_A}{P_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{mRT}{32 V_A}}{\dfrac{mRT}{4 V_A}} = \dfrac{4}{32} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

The ratio of gas pressure in A to that in B is $1:8$.

Answer: $1:8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 1 kg of water at $100^{}^{\circ}$ C is converted to steam at the same temperature. Volume of 1 cc of water changes to $1671 \times 10^3$ cc on boiling. The change in internal energy of the system is (Latent Heat of vaporisation of water is $22.68 \times 10^5\ J\ kg^{-1}$; 1 atm $= 1.0 \times 10^5$ Pa)
questions.solution:
Given the final volume of 1 kg of steam is $1671 \times 10^3$ cc $= 1.671$ m^3$.

Initial volume of 1 kg of water is $1000$ cc $= 10^{-3}$ m^3$.

Change in volume, $\Delta V = 1.671 - 0.001 = 1.670$ m^3$.

Work done, $W = P\Delta V = 1.0 \times 10^5 \times 1.670 = 1.67 \times 10^5$ J.

Heat supplied, $Q = mL = 1 \times 22.68 \times 10^5 = 22.68 \times 10^5$ J.

Using the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$.

$\Delta U = Q - W = 22.68 \times 10^5 - 1.67 \times 10^5 = 21.01 \times 10^5$ J.

Answer: $21.01 \times 10^5\ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermal source supplies heat at a rate of $300 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$. By using that heat a system performs work at a rate of $125 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$. What is the rate at which the internal energy of the system increases?
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the rate of heat supplied to the system is equal to the sum of the rate of work done by the system and the rate of change of internal energy of the system.

Let $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$ be the rate of heat supply, $\dfrac{dW}{dt}$ be the rate of work done, and $\dfrac{dU}{dt}$ be the rate of change of internal energy.

The equation is given by $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dW}{dt} + \dfrac{dU}{dt}$.

Given values are $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 300 \text{ Js}^{-1}$ and $\dfrac{dW}{dt} = 125 \text{ Js}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$300 = 125 + \dfrac{dU}{dt}$

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 300 - 125 = 175 \text{ Js}^{-1}$.

Answer: $175 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monoatomic ideal gas, initially at temperature $T_1$, is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston. The gas is allowed to expand adiabatically to a temperature $T_2$ by releasing the piston suddenly. If $L$ and $2 L$ are the lengths of the gas column before and after expansion respectively, then $\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}$ is
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process of an ideal gas, the relationship between temperature and volume is given by $T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$.

For a monoatomic gas, the adiabatic index $\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$. Thus, $\gamma - 1 = \dfrac{5}{3} - 1 = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

The volume of the gas is proportional to the length of the gas column, $V \propto L$. Therefore, $T_1 L_1^{2/3} = T_2 L_2^{2/3}$.

Given $L_1 = L$ and $L_2 = 2L$, we have $T_1 L^{2/3} = T_2 (2L)^{2/3}$.

Rearranging to find the ratio $\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}$:

$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{(2L)^{2/3}}{L^{2/3}} = \left(\dfrac{2L}{L}\right)^{2/3} = 2^{2/3}$.

Answer: $2^{2 / 3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is expanding such that $P T^2=$ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is
questions.solution:
The equation of state for an ideal gas is $PV = nRT$.

Given $PT^{2} = C$, where $C$ is a constant, we can write $P = C T^{-2}$.

Substituting this into the ideal gas equation, we get $(C T^{-2}) V = nRT$.

Rearranging for $V$, we have $V = \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{3}$.

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{dV}{dT} \right)_{P}$.

Differentiating $V$ with respect to $T$ from the relation $V = \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{3}$, we get $\dfrac{dV}{dT} = 3 \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{2}$.

Substituting $V$ and $\dfrac{dV}{dT}$ into the expression for $\gamma$:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{3} \right)} \left( 3 \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{T}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The heat required to increase the temperature of 4 moles of a mono-atomic ideal gas from $273^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $473^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ at constant volume is
questions.solution:
The heat required at constant volume is given by the formula $Q = n C_{v} \Delta T$.

For a mono-atomic ideal gas, the molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_{v} = \dfrac{3}{2} R$.

Given values are $n = 4$ moles, $T_{1} = 273^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$, and $T_{2} = 473^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$.

The change in temperature is $\Delta T = T_{2} - T_{1} = 473 - 273 = 200 \text{ K}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$Q = 4 \times \left( \dfrac{3}{2} R \right) \times 200$

$Q = 4 \times 1.5 R \times 200$

$Q = 6 R \times 200 = 1200 R$.

Answer: 1200 R

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
$A given volume of gas at NTP is allowed to expand 6 times of its original volume, first under isothermal condition and then under adiabatic condition. Which of the given statement is correct?
[Given \dfrac{C_p}{C_v}=\gamma=1.4$ ]
options: The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.
Pressure remains same in both adiabatic and isothermal expansion
The final temperature after the adiabatic expansion is 1.4 times less than the final temperature after the isothermal expansion.
The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is 1.4 times greater than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.
questions.solution:
Let the initial pressure be $P_0$, initial volume be $V_0$, and initial temperature be $T_0$. The gas expands to a final volume $V_f = 6V_0$.

For isothermal expansion, the final pressure $P_{iso}$ is given by $P_0 V_0 = P_{iso} (6V_0)$, which gives $P_{iso} = \dfrac{P_0}{6}$.

For adiabatic expansion, the final pressure $P_{adia}$ is given by $P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_{adia} (6V_0)^{\gamma}$, which gives $P_{adia} = P_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{\gamma}$.

Given $\gamma = 1.4$, we have $P_{adia} = P_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{1.4}$.

Comparing $P_{iso} = P_0 (6)^{-1}$ and $P_{adia} = P_0 (6)^{-1.4}$, since $6^{1.4} > 6^1$, it follows that $\dfrac{1}{6^{1.4}} < \dfrac{1}{6^1}$.

Therefore, $P_{adia} < P_{iso}$. The final pressure after adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after isothermal expansion.

Answer: The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample of an ideal gas is taken through the cyclic process ABCA as shown in figure below. It absorbs 60J of heat during the part AB and rejects 80 J of heat during CA. There is no heat exchanged during the process BC. A work of 40 J is done on the gas during the part BC. If the internal energy of the gas at A is 1450 J , then the work done by the gas during the part CA is:
questions.solution:
The process is a cycle ABCA. We are given the heat exchange $Q$ and work done $W$ for each part of the cycle.

For process AB: $Q_{AB} = 60$ J. Since $W_{AB} = 0$ (as it is a vertical line on the P-V diagram, volume is constant), the change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{AB} = Q_{AB} - W_{AB} = 60 - 0 = 60$ J. Thus, $U_B - U_A = 60$ J.

For process BC: $Q_{BC} = 0$ J. Work is done on the gas, so $W_{BC} = -40$ J. The change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{BC} = Q_{BC} - W_{BC} = 0 - (-40) = 40$ J. Thus, $U_C - U_B = 40$ J.

For process CA: $Q_{CA} = -80$ J (heat is rejected). Let $W_{CA}$ be the work done by the gas during CA. The change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{CA} = Q_{CA} - W_{CA} = -80 - W_{CA}$.

Since the process is cyclic, the total change in internal energy over the cycle is zero: $\Delta U_{AB} + \Delta U_{BC} + \Delta U_{CA} = 0$.

Substituting the values: $60 + 40 + (-80 - W_{CA}) = 0$.

$100 - 80 - W_{CA} = 0$.

$20 - W_{CA} = 0 \Rightarrow W_{CA} = 20$ J.

Answer: 20 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of specific heat capacities at constant pressure to that at constant volume for a given mass of a gas is $\dfrac{5}{2}$. If the percentage increase in volume of the gas while undergoing an adiabatic change is $\dfrac{3}{2}$, then the percentage decrease in pressure will be:
questions.solution:
The ratio of specific heat capacities is given as $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v} = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure and volume is $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Taking the logarithmic derivative, we get $\dfrac{dP}{P} + \gamma \dfrac{dV}{V} = 0$, which implies $\dfrac{dP}{P} = -\gamma \dfrac{dV}{V}$.

The percentage increase in volume is $\dfrac{dV}{V} \times 100 = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5$.

Substituting the values, the percentage change in pressure is $\dfrac{dP}{P} \times 100 = -\gamma \times \left( \dfrac{dV}{V} \times 100 \right) = -\dfrac{5}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{2} = -\dfrac{15}{4}$.

The negative sign indicates a decrease in pressure. Thus, the percentage decrease in pressure is $\dfrac{15}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{15}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The molar heat capacity in a process of a diatomic gas if it does a work of $\frac{Q}{4}$, when a heat of $Q$ is supplied to it is
questions.solution:
$d U=C_V d T=\left(\frac{5}{2} R\right) d T$ or $d T=\frac{2(d U)}{5 R}$
From first law of thermodynamics,
$d U=d Q-d W=Q-\frac{Q}{4}=\frac{3 Q}{4}$
Now, molar heat capacity,
$C=\frac{d Q}{d T}=\frac{Q}{\frac{2(d U)}{5 R}}=\frac{5 R Q}{2\left(\frac{3 Q}{4}\right)}=\frac{10}{3} R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermally insulated rigid container contains an ideal gas heated by a filament of resistance $100 \Omega$ through a current of 1 A for 5 min , then change in internal energy is
questions.solution:
Volume of the ideal gas is constant, so $W=0$.
Using first law of thermodynamics,
$\begin{aligned} \\ \Delta Q & =\Delta U \Rightarrow \Delta U=i^2 R t \\ \\ & =1^2 \times 100 \times 5 \times 60 \\ \\ & =30 \times 10^3=30 \mathrm{ kJ} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermodynamic system changes its state from A to C in two different paths ABC and AC. The internal energy of the system at state C is $20\text{ J}$ and at state A is $10\text{ J}$. Heat supplied to the system to go from A to C along path AC is
questions.solution:
$\Delta U = U_C - U_A = 20 - 10 = 10$ J (state function, path independent)

Work done along path AC (area of trapezium under P-V curve):

$W_{AC} = \dfrac{1}{2}(P_A + P_C)(V_C - V_A) = \dfrac{1}{2}(5+15)(9-3) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 6 = 60$ J

By first law: $Q_{AC} = \Delta U + W_{AC} = 10 + 60 = 70$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder of fixed capacity 44.81 contains hydrogen gas at STP. What is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of the gas in the cylinder by $20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ ? ($R=8.31 \mathrm{ J} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
At STP, the volume of 1 mole of an ideal gas is $22.4 \text{ L}$.

Given the volume of the cylinder is $44.8 \text{ L}$, the number of moles $n$ of hydrogen gas is $n = \dfrac{44.8}{22.4} = 2 \text{ moles}$.

Hydrogen is a diatomic gas, so its molar heat capacity at constant volume $C_V$ is given by $C_V = \dfrac{f}{2}R$, where $f = 5$ is the degrees of freedom for a diatomic molecule.

$C_V = \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1} = 20.775 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.

The heat required $Q$ to raise the temperature by $\Delta T = 20^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$ (which is equivalent to $20 \text{ K}$) at constant volume is $Q = n C_V \Delta T$.

$Q = 2 \times 20.775 \times 20 = 40 \times 20.775 = 831 \text{ J}$.

Answer: 831 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is $2240 \mathrm{ J}$. If the work done in the process of vaporisation of $1 \mathrm{ g}$ is $168 \mathrm{ J}$, the increase in internal energy is
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the heat supplied $Q$ is equal to the sum of the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ and the work done $W$ by the system during the process of vaporisation.

$Q = \Delta U + W$

Given that the latent heat of vaporisation $L = 2240 \text{ J}$ for $1 \text{ g}$ of water, the heat supplied $Q$ is $2240 \text{ J}$.

The work done $W$ during the process is given as $168 \text{ J}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$2240 \text{ J} = \Delta U + 168 \text{ J}$

Solving for the change in internal energy $\Delta U$:

$\Delta U = 2240 \text{ J} - 168 \text{ J}$

$\Delta U = 2072 \text{ J}$

Answer: 2072 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is taken through the cycle $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$, as shown in figure. What is the net work done by the gas?
questions.solution:
Net work done by the gas $=$ Area enclosed in $p-V$ curve, i.e. area of $\triangle A B C$.
$W_{\text{net }}=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{ J}=10^3 \mathrm{ J}=1000 $$\mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas goes from state $A$ to state $B$ via three different processes as indicated in the $p-V$ diagram. If $Q_1, Q_2$ and $Q_3$ indicate the heat absorbed by the three processes and $\Delta U_1, \Delta U_2$ and $\Delta U_3$ indicate the change in internal energy along the three processes respectively, then
options: $Q_1 > Q_2 > Q_3$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 > Q_2 > Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 > Q_2 > Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1 > \Delta U_2 > \Delta U_3$
questions.solution:
For all processes 1,2 and 3
Change in internal energy, i.e.
\begin{gathered}
\Delta U=U_B-U_A \\
\therefore \Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3 \Rightarrow Q=\Delta U+\Delta W
\end{gathered}$
Now, \Delta W=$ work done by the gas, i.e. area under $p-V$ curve.
As, area $(1) > $ area $(2) > $ area $(3)\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \Delta W_1 > \Delta W_2 > \Delta W_3 \\
\therefore & Q_1 > Q_2 > Q_3
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $150 \mathrm{ J}$ of heat is added to a system and the work done by the system is $110 \mathrm{ J}$, then change in internal energy will be

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an adiabatic expansion of air, the volume is increased by $6.2 \%$. The percentage change in pressure is $(\gamma=1.4)$
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure $P$ and volume $V$ is given by $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Taking the logarithmic differentiation of the equation $PV^{\gamma} = C$, we get $\ln P + \gamma \ln V = \ln C$.

Differentiating both sides, we obtain $\dfrac{dP}{P} + \gamma \dfrac{dV}{V} = 0$, which implies $\dfrac{dP}{P} = -\gamma \dfrac{dV}{V}$.

Given that the volume increases by $6.2 \%$, we have $\dfrac{dV}{V} = 0.062$.

Substituting the values $\gamma = 1.4$ and $\dfrac{dV}{V} = 0.062$ into the expression for the fractional change in pressure:

$\dfrac{dP}{P} = -1.4 \times 0.062 = -0.0868$.

The percentage change in pressure is $\dfrac{dP}{P} \times 100 = -0.0868 \times 100 = -8.68 \%$.

The magnitude of the percentage change in pressure is $8.68 \%$.

Answer: 8.68

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the ratio of specific heat of a gas at constant pressure to that at constant volume is $\gamma$, the change in internal energy of a mass of a gas when the volume changes from $\mathrm{V}$ to $3 \mathrm{ V}$ at constant pressure is
questions.solution:
The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ for an ideal gas is given by the formula $\Delta U = n C_{v} \Delta T$.

For an ideal gas, $C_{v} = \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1}$. Thus, $\Delta U = n \left( \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1} \right) \Delta T$.

Using the ideal gas law $PV = nRT$, at constant pressure $P$, we have $P \Delta V = nR \Delta T$.

Substituting $nR \Delta T = P \Delta V$ into the expression for internal energy, we get $\Delta U = \dfrac{P \Delta V}{\gamma - 1}$.

Given the volume changes from $V$ to $3V$, the change in volume is $\Delta V = 3V - V = 2V$.

Therefore, $\Delta U = \dfrac{P(2V)}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{2PV}{\gamma - 1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 P V}{(\gamma-1)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is taken through the cycle $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$, as shown in figure. What is the net work done by the gas?
questions.solution:
Net work done = area enclosed in P-V diagram. Cycle $A \to B \to C \to A$ is clockwise \to work done is positive.

The enclosed area is a right-angled triangle.

Base $= V_C - V_A = (7 - 3) \times 10^{-3} = 4 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^3$

Height $= P_B - P_C = (6 - 2) \times 10^5 = 4 \times 10^5$ Pa

$W_{net} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 10^5 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 10^2 = 800$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $150 \mathrm{ J}$ of heat is added to a system and the work done by the system is $110 \mathrm{ J}$, then change in internal energy will be
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ is given by the equation:

$\Delta U = Q - W$

where $Q$ is the heat added to the system and $W$ is the work done by the system.

Given values are $Q = 150 \text{ J}$ and $W = 110 \text{ J}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$\Delta U = 150 \text{ J} - 110 \text{ J} = 40 \text{ J}$

Answer: 40 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas goes from state $A$ to state $B$ via three different processes as indicated in the $p$-$V$ diagram. If $Q_1, Q_2$ and $Q_3$ indicate the heat absorbed by the three processes and $\Delta U_1, \Delta U_2$ and $\Delta U_3$ indicate the change in internal energy along the three processes respectively, then
options: $Q_1 > Q_2 > Q_3$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 > Q_2 > Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 > Q_2 > Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1 > \Delta U_2 > \Delta U_3$
questions.solution:
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, which is a state function. Since all three processes start at state A and end at state B, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ is the same for all three paths. Therefore, $\Delta U_1 = \Delta U_2 = \Delta U_3$.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$, where $W$ is the work done by the gas. The work done $W$ is equal to the area under the $p-V$ curve. From the given diagram, the area under path 1 is the largest, followed by path 2, and then path 3. Thus, $W_1 > W_2 > W_3$.

Since $\Delta U$ is constant for all paths, the heat absorbed $Q$ follows the same order as the work done $W$. Therefore, $Q_1 > Q_2 > Q_3$.

Answer: $Q_1 > Q_2 > Q_3$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a Carnot heat engine has a sink at a temperature of $27^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ and takes $100\text{ kcal}$ of heat from a source at a temperature of $627^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$, the work done (in J) is:
questions.solution:
$T_2 = 27 + 273 = 300\,\text{K}$, $T_1 = 627 + 273 = 900\,\text{K}$

$\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{900} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$Q_1 = 100\,\text{kcal} = 10^5 \times 4.2\,\text{J} = 4.2 \times 10^5\,\text{J}$

$W = \eta \times Q_1 = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 4.2 \times 10^5 = 2.8 \times 10^5 = 0.28 \times 10^6\,\text{J}$

Correct option: (1)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the following $p$-V diagram, an ideal gas undergoing a change of state from $A$ to $B$. Four different processes I, II, III and IV as shown in the figure may lead to same change of state.
options: Work done is minimum in case II
Change in internal energy is same in all the four cases
Change in internal energy is same in IV and III cases, but not in I and II
questions.solution:
The internal energy $U$ of an ideal gas is a state function, which depends only on the temperature $T$ of the gas. For an ideal gas, the internal energy is given by $U = \dfrac{f}{2} nRT$, where $f$ is the degrees of freedom.

Since the change of state is from $A$ to $B$ in all four processes, the initial state $(P_A, V_A, T_A)$ and the final state $(P_B, V_B, T_B)$ are the same for all paths.

The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ is given by $\Delta U = U_B - U_A = \dfrac{f}{2} nR(T_B - T_A)$.

Because $T_A$ and $T_B$ are fixed for all four processes, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ must be the same for all four processes I, II, III, and IV.

Answer: Change in internal energy is same in all the four cases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is taken through the cycle $A \to B \to C \to A$, as shown in the figure (assume Volume $V$ is in $m^3$). If the net heat supplied to the gas in the cycle is 5 J, the work done by the gas in the process $C \to A$ is,
questions.solution:
For a complete cycle, $\Delta U_{net} = 0$, so by the first law: $W_{net} = Q_{net} = 5$ J

$W_{net} = W_{A \to B} + W_{B \to C} + W_{C \to A}$

Process $A \to B$: Constant pressure $p = 10$ N/m^2$, volume increases from $V_A = 1$ m^3$ to $V_B = 2$ m^3$
$W_{A \to B} = p\Delta V = 10 \times (2-1) = 10$ J

Process $B \to C$: Constant volume (\Delta V = 0$)
$W_{B \to C} = 0$ J

Substituting:
5 = 10 + 0 + W_{C \to A}$
$W_{C \to A} = -5 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: There are two identical containers $C_1$ and $C_2$ containing to identical gases. Gas in $C_1$ is reduced to half of its original volume adiabatically, while the gas in container $C_2$ is also reduced to half of its initial volume isothermally. Find the ratio of final pressure in these containers. (\gamma$ be the adiabatic constant).$
questions.solution:
Let the initial pressure and volume of the gas in both containers be $P_0$ and $V_0$ respectively.

For container $C_1$, the process is adiabatic. The relation between pressure and volume is $P V^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Given the final volume $V_1 = \dfrac{V_0}{2}$, the final pressure $P_1$ is given by $P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_1 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{2} \right)^{\gamma}$.

$P_1 = P_0 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{V_0/2} \right)^{\gamma} = P_0 (2)^{\gamma}$.

For container $C_2$, the process is isothermal. The relation between pressure and volume is $P V = \text{constant}$.

Given the final volume $V_2 = \dfrac{V_0}{2}$, the final pressure $P_2$ is given by $P_0 V_0 = P_2 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{2} \right).

$P_2 = P_0 $\left( \dfrac{V_0}{V_0/2} \right) =$2 P_0$.

The ratio of final pressures is \dfrac{P_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{P_0 2^{\gamma}}{2 P_0} = \dfrac{2^{\gamma}}{2} =$2^{\gamma-$1}$.

Thus, the ratio is $2^{\gamma-$1} : 1$.

Answer: $2^{\gamma-$1}: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an adiabatic process with the ratio of two specific heat, $\gamma=\dfrac{3}{2}$, pressure is increased by $\dfrac{2}{3} \%$, then decrease in the volume will be
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure $P$ and volume $V$ is given by $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides, we get $\ln P + \gamma \ln V = \text{constant}$.

Differentiating both sides, we obtain $\dfrac{dP}{P} + \gamma \dfrac{dV}{V} = 0$, which implies $\dfrac{dV}{V} = -\dfrac{1}{\gamma} \dfrac{dP}{P}$.

Given $\gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}$ and the percentage increase in pressure $\dfrac{dP}{P} = \dfrac{2}{3} \%$.

Substituting these values, the percentage change in volume is $\dfrac{dV}{V} = -\dfrac{1}{3/2} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \% = -\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \% = -\dfrac{4}{9} \%$.

The negative sign indicates a decrease in volume. Therefore, the decrease in volume is $\dfrac{4}{9} \%$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{9} \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For an ideal gas, coefficient of volume expansion is given by
questions.solution:
The equation of state for an ideal gas is $PV = nRT$.

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P}$.

From the ideal gas equation, $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$.

Differentiating $V$ with respect to $T$ at constant pressure $P$, we get $\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P} = \dfrac{nR}{P}$.

Substituting this into the expression for $\gamma$, we have $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{nR}{P} \right)$.

Since $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$, we can write $\dfrac{nR}{P} = \dfrac{V}{T}$.

Therefore, $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{V}{T} \right) = \dfrac{1}{T}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Carnot cycle of an engine is given below

Total work done by the gas in one cycle is
questions.solution:
The Carnot cycle has two isothermal and two adiabatic processes.

$P \to Q$: Isothermal expansion at $T_1$ ($T_1 = T_2$): $W_{PQ} = \mu RT_1 \ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$

$Q \to R$: Adiabatic expansion: $W_{QR} = \dfrac{\mu R(T_2 - T_3)}{\gamma - 1}$

$R \to S$: Isothermal compression at $T_3$ ($T_3 = T_4$): $W_{RS} = -\mu RT_3 \ln\dfrac{V_3}{V_4}$

$S \to P$: Adiabatic compression: $W_{SP} = \dfrac{\mu R(T_4 - T_1)}{\gamma - 1}$

Since $T_1 = T_2$ and $T_3 = T_4$, the adiabatic work terms cancel: $W_{QR} + W_{SP} = 0$

Total work: $W = \mu RT_1 \ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} - \mu RT_3 \ln\dfrac{V_3}{V_4}$

$= \mu RT_1 \log\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} - \mu RT_2 \log\dfrac{V_3}{V_4}$

Correct option: (2)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $1 \mathrm{ mm}^{3}$ of a gas is compressed at 1 atmospheric pressure and temperature $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $627^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. What is the final pressure under adiabatic condition? $(\gamma$ for the gas $=15$ )
questions.solution:
Given, $V_{1}=1 \mathrm{ mm}^{3} \begin{aligned}&=10^{-9} \mathrm{ m}^{3}\\
p_{1} &=1 \mathrm{ atm}\\
&=1 \times10^{5} \mathrm{ N}/ \mathrmm^{2} \\
T_{1} &=27+273 \\
&=300 \mathrm{ K}\\
T_{2} &=627+273 \\
&=900 \mathrm{ K}
\end{aligned}$ Under adiabatic condition, $\begin{aligned}& p_{1}^{1-\gamma} T_{1}^{\gamma}=p_{2}^{1-\gamma} T_{2}^{\gamma} \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\right)^{1-\gamma}&=\left(\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}\right)^{\gamma}\\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\right)^{1-1.5}&=\left(\frac{300}{900}\right)^{1.5}\\
\Rightarrow \quad &\left(\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\right)^{-0.5}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{1.5}\\
\Rightarrow \quad &\left(\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}\right)^{0.5}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{1.5}
\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\frac{15}{05}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{27}\Rightarrow \quad p_{2}=27 p_{1}=27 \times 1 \times 10^{5}=27 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{ N} / \mathrmm^{2}$

questions.solution:

\therefore \text{ Efficiency, } \eta&=1-\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\\

&=\frac{39}{273}\\
&=0.142 \\
&=14.2 \%
\end{aligned}
$

questions.solution:
Work done in a cyclic process is equal to the area enclosed by the cycle in $p-V$ diagram.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad W &=\text{ Area } A B C D \\
&=A B \times A D \\
&=(2 p-p) \times(2 V-V)=p \times V=p V

questions.q: Carnot heat engine takes $300 \mathrm{ J}$ of heat from a source at $627^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and gives some part of it to $\operatorname{sink}$ at $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. Work done by engine in one cycle is
questions.solution:
The efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by
$\eta=1-\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}$
Given, $\quad T_{1}=627^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=627+273=900 \mathrm{ K}$
and $\quad T_{2}=27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=27+273=300 \mathrm{ K}\Rightarrow \quad \eta=1-\frac{300}{900}=\frac{600}{900}=\frac{2}{3}$
Also, $\quad \eta=\frac{\text{ Work done }}{\text{ Heat taken }}\Rightarrow$ Work done $=\eta \times$ Heat taken
$=\frac{2}{3} \times 300=200 \mathrm{ J}$

volume remains constant and no work is done by the system
Both volume and work done changes
questions.solution:
In isochoric process, volume of the system remains constant.
i.e. $\quad \Delta V=V_{1}-V_{2}=V-V=0 \quad  \left[\becauseV_{1}=V_{2}=V\right]$
Hence, work done, $W=p \times \Delta V=p \times0=0$
